source: USDA ARS Tobacco Pathology Research Unit / North Carolina State University / University of Kentucky Extension Tobacco IPM
title: Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV, Tobamovirus, Virgaviridae) on Cultivated Tobacco
content: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV; species Tobacco mosaic virus, genus Tobamovirus, family Virgaviridae, order Martellivirales) is historically the most intensively studied, best-understood, and most famous plant virus in the world - the first virus ever to be discovered (Iwanowski 1892, Beijerinck 1898), the first virus to be purified and crystallized (Wendell Stanley 1935, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1946), the first virus to have its genome completely sequenced (Goelet et al. 1982, 6395 nucleotide positive-sense single-stranded monopartite RNA genome), and the model system upon which many of the fundamental principles of modern virology, molecular biology, and plant pathology are based. TMV is the type member of the genus Tobamovirus (the name derives from 'tobacco mosaic' virus = TobaMoVirus), which includes > 40 related species of extremely stable, mechanically transmitted, positive-sense RNA plant viruses with rigid, rod-shaped virions. TMV infects > 350 species of plants in > 40 families worldwide including solanaceous crops (tobacco Nicotiana tabacum L., tomato Solanum lycopersicum, pepper Capsicum annuum, potato S. tuberosum, eggplant S. melongena, petunia Petunia x hybrida), cucurbits (cucumber, melon, squash), legumes (common bean Phaseolus vulgaris, pea Pisum sativum, soybean Glycine max, alfalfa Medicago sativa, clover Trifolium spp.), chenopodiaceous plants (sugar beet Beta vulgaris, spinach Spinacia oleracea, Chenopodium amaranticolor), brassicas (turnip, rutabaga), and many ornamental, weed, and wild plant species. TMV is the most economically important viral disease of cultivated flue-cured, burley, dark-fired, dark-air-cured, cigar-wrapper, and oriental tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum L.) worldwide, wherever tobacco is grown commercially on a large scale (China, India, Brazil, the United States, Zimbabwe, Malawi, Turkey, Indonesia, Russia, Ukraine, Cuba, Dominican Republic). Annual tobacco production losses from TMV are estimated at approximately 100-150 million USD globally (2023); individual field infections can reduce cured leaf yield by 10-40% and significantly reduce cured leaf quality (color, body, and aroma chemistry - 'body', 'finish', and smoking flavor attributes), resulting in grade rejection or significant price downgrading at auction or contract delivery. TMV infection of cigar-wrapper tobacco (Connecticut shade-grown, Ecuadorian, Cuban, Dominican, Indonesian wrapper types) is particularly damaging because even mild mosaic leaf discoloration completely destroys the cosmetic commercial value of the wrapper leaf, which is the highest-value per-pound tobacco product in the global market. The characteristic and diagnostic symptoms of Tobacco mosaic virus infection on flue-cured and burley tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum L.) develop systemically on the upper, newly expanding leaves approximately 7-21 days after initial inoculation, depending on host age, virus isolate, and temperature. Young newly infected plants (4-8 leaf stage) are most severely affected: the characteristic 'mosaic' pattern on the leaf blade consists of a patchy, irregular mottling or checkerboard-like alternation of contrasting areas of deep normal-green tissue (areas where the TMV 126 kDa replicase suppresses the plant's RNA-silencing defense via the p126 VSR suppressor of gene silencing function) and areas of light green, pale yellow, or yellowish chlorotic tissue (areas where the host's N-gene-mediated hypersensitive defense has not yet been activated, or where host metabolism has been disrupted by TMV replicase and movement protein MP activity). On rapidly growing young leaves of susceptible tobacco cultivars, this mosaic pattern is often accompanied by severe leaf malformation including downward curling of leaf margins, cupping, epinasty, twisting, rugosity (crinkling, bumpy 'puckered' raised blisters on the lamina caused by unequal cell division rates in infected vs. non-infected leaf sectors), narrowing ('shoestringing' or 'fern leaf' distortion), and overall severe stunting of the entire plant's growth. Infected plants that are mechanically topped (removal of the terminal inflorescence to stimulate axillary 'sucker' growth) often develop severe mosaic symptoms on the sucker leaves that regrow after topping. On older, mid-season plants infected after the 10-leaf stage, symptoms are usually much milder: only a subtle light-green mosaic mottle may appear on the uppermost 2-3 leaves, with little or no leaf malformation or stunting. TMV does not usually cause necrosis or death of infected tobacco plants; however, certain hypervirulent 'yellow' TMV strains (TMV-Y, TMV-Vulgaris-U1, TMV-type OM) can cause necrosis of the veins and petioles of very young seedlings on highly susceptible cultivars at temperatures above 30 C. Cigar-wrapper and aromatic shade-grown tobacco cultivars develop a characteristic severe mosaic known in the industry as 'green spot' or 'mottle spot': distinct circular to irregular spots of light-green or yellowish tissue 3-10 mm in diameter scattered across otherwise dark-green wrapper-grade leaves - these spots remain visible even after curing and fermenting the leaf and are an automatic cause of grade rejection for wrapper leaf. The TMV virion particle is extremely stable - one of the most stable and environmentally resistant of all known plant viruses. Purified TMV virions remain infectious after 50 years stored dry at room temperature; dried TMV-infected tobacco tissue (cigarettes, pipe tobacco, chewing tobacco, snuff, cured cigar leaf) retains infectivity for DECADES; TMV is resistant to 95% ethanol, chloroform, ether, acetone, 10% formalin, and pH values between 2 and 10; it survives heating to 90-93 C for 10 minutes in crude plant sap, and dry-heat resistance up to 120 C; it is also resistant to many common commercial disinfectants. The virion is a rigid, right-handed helical rod approximately 300 nm long by 18 nm in diameter, consisting of ~ 2130 copies of a single 17.5 kDa capsid protein (CP) subunit arranged around a 6400 nt positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome. TMV is transmitted by three main mechanisms: (1) MECHANICAL TRANSMISSION (the primary natural method): TMV is extremely easily transmitted by simple mechanical contact between plants ('rubbing') when virions on contaminated plant surfaces, hands, clothing, tools, equipment, or soil particles come into contact with small micro-wounds on the leaf trichomes, epidermal cells, or petioles of healthy tobacco plants; the extremely high stability of TMV particles allows this mechanical transmission to occur at extremely high efficiency. In commercial tobacco fields, mechanical transmission is the dominant mechanism of within-field and between-plant spread: workers walk through fields performing cultivation operations (hand-hoeing, topping, suckering, harvesting, tying, or grading), their hands and clothing become contaminated with TMV particles from an infected plant, and subsequent contact with healthy plants mechanically inoculates the virus at a rate of up to 100% of subsequently handled plants within a single day. TMV contamination on workers' hands and on pruning shears / topping knives remains infectious for hours even after washing with plain soap and water (TMV virions are not enveloped, so standard soap does not inactivate them - this is a key epidemiological point). (2) SEED TRANSMISSION: TMV can be carried externally on the seed coat (testa) of tobacco seed at rates of 0.1-5% depending on cultivar and harvest date; this is a minor source of inoculum but historically was the mechanism of international long-distance spread of TMV to new tobacco-growing regions. (3) INDIRECT HUMAN TRANSMISSION: smokers (cigarettes, cigars, pipe tobacco) and chewers of TMV-infected tobacco products have TMV on their fingers constantly; a smoker who handles tobacco transplants, pepper transplants, or tomato transplants after smoking a single cigarette can mechanically transmit TMV to every plant they subsequently touch. This route of transmission is particularly important in transplant greenhouses, where a single worker with TMV-contaminated fingers can inoculate hundreds of greenhouse tobacco, pepper, and tomato seedlings within a few hours. Critically, TMV is NOT transmitted by aphids, whiteflies, thrips, leafhoppers, mites, nematodes, or any other arthropod vector (Tobamoviruses have no known biological vectors - they are strictly mechanically transmitted by contact). TMV is also NOT transmitted by dodder (Cuscuta), by soil fungi, or by pollen. Management of Tobacco mosaic virus in tobacco and other crops relies EXCLUSIVELY on PREVENTION, EXCLUSION, SANITATION, and GENETIC RESISTANCE - there are NO curative chemical or biological treatments available that can eliminate or reduce TMV infection once a plant is systemically infected. (1) GENETIC RESISTANCE is the most effective and economical control measure: the dominant N gene from Nicotiana glutinosa L. (a diploid wild tobacco species from Peru) has been bred into > 99% of modern commercial flue-cured, burley, Maryland, and dark-tobacco cultivars currently grown in the United States, Canada, Brazil, southern Africa, and China. The N gene (a Toll-interleukin-1 receptor / nucleotide-binding site / leucine-rich repeat TIR-NB-LRR class R gene) confers extreme hypersensitive-response (HR) immunity to nearly all common strains of TMV: when a TMV particle inoculates a plant carrying the N gene, the p50 helicase domain of the TMV 126/183 kDa replicase protein is directly or indirectly recognized by the N receptor protein, triggering a rapid, localized, programmed cell death (HR necrotic lesion) at the point of entry within 24-48 hours (visible as a distinct, dry, round, dark brown necrotic local lesion 1-3 mm in diameter on the inoculated leaf). This HR hypersensitive reaction completely halts all further movement of TMV out of the local lesion and into the vascular system, so the entire rest of the plant remains completely free of systemic mosaic symptoms; this is called 'local-lesion-forming resistance' or 'TMV immunity' in tobacco breeding terminology. The N gene has been deployed commercially since the 1930s and has remained effective against all common TMV strains for > 90 years - it is one of the most durable plant R genes ever bred into any crop (this durability is because the TMV replicase p50 helicase domain that N recognizes is an essential, irreplaceable core function of the virus that cannot mutate without eliminating TMV viability). Note: the N gene is temperature-sensitive; at sustained air temperatures above 28-30 C (82-86 F), the hypersensitive response is suppressed, and N-gene-carrying tobacco plants may develop systemic mosaic symptoms when temperatures are very high for extended periods. A small number of TMV resistance-breaking isolates have been very rarely described in the literature, but none have become established in commercial fields to date. The N' gene from Nicotiana sylvestris, the Tm-2^2 gene from Solanum peruvianum, and the L genes from Capsicum chacoense provide TMV resistance in tomato and pepper cultivars respectively. (2) EXCLUSION via virus-tested certified clean seed and clean transplants is mandatory: (a) plant ONLY certified tobacco seed that has been produced under official inspection and tested free of TMV contamination by ELISA, RT-PCR, or local-lesion assay on Nicotiana tabacum 'Xanthi nc' or Chenopodium amaranticolor bioindicator plants. Seed-borne TMV can be effectively eliminated from tobacco seed by a standard 10-minute soak in a 10% (w/v) aqueous solution of trisodium phosphate (Na3PO4, TSP = tri-sodium phosphate, the classic virological disinfectant) at room temperature, followed by three rinses in clean tap water; this 10% TSP treatment denatures the TMV coat protein on the seed surface and inactivates > 99.99% of seed-borne TMV infectivity with no effect on seed germination. (b) produce tobacco transplants in sanitized greenhouses or float-bed systems located at least 500 m away from any previous-year tobacco fields, old curing barns, tobacco storage warehouses, or tobacco packing houses; never produce transplants in the same greenhouse where cured tobacco products are handled or stored. (3) SANITATION AND DISINFESTATION protocols are the core of TMV management in both transplant greenhouses and production fields, especially in operations growing TMV-susceptible (non-N-gene) cigar-wrapper and oriental tobacco cultivars. The key rules are: (a) PROHIBIT ALL SMOKING of any tobacco product (cigarettes, cigars, pipe, chewing) inside transplant greenhouses, float-bed systems, or during any field operation involving handling of live tobacco plants (topping, suckering, hoeing, harvesting, grading). (b) implement mandatory hand-washing and hand-disinfection stations using 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP, Na3PO4, the gold standard TMV disinfectant) or 20% (w/v) powdered non-fat dry milk (NFDM) solution (the casein phosphoproteins in milk physically bind and neutralize TMV particles on skin, as effectively as TSP) at every entry point to the transplant house and at every field entry point. Workers must wash their hands and forearms thoroughly in 10% TSP or 20% non-fat milk solution for a minimum of 30 seconds BEFORE touching any live tobacco or tomato/pepper plants, and again every 20 minutes during handling operations. (c) all cutting tools (topping knives, pruning shears, machetes, suckering pliers, harvester sickle bars) must be soaked or continuously dipped in a recirculating bath of 10% TSP or 20% NFDM or 6% household bleach (0.5% sodium hypochlorite, NaOCl) during use. (d) greenhouse transplant trays, styrofoam float trays, plastic seedling flats, greenhouse benches, and walkways must be steam-sterilized (85 C for 30 minutes minimum) OR pressure-washed then soaked in 10% TSP for 30 minutes between production cycles. (e) in transplant greenhouses and tobacco nurseries, work only from known healthy blocks toward potentially infected blocks; never go back from a suspected TMV-infected area into a clean area without full sanitation. If a plant is found with TMV mosaic symptoms in a greenhouse, remove the entire plant plus the 5 plants on each side of it (or remove the entire flat) into a sealed plastic bag for autoclaving or incineration immediately, then sanitize all hands and tools before continuing work. (4) CULTURAL PRACTICES: (a) separate transplant production from all cured-tobacco product handling and storage (cigar boxes, cured bales, cigarette manufacturing, etc.) by a minimum of 500 m and by separate personnel. (b) avoid unnecessary mechanical handling (excessive topping, unnecessary leaf touching) of tobacco during periods of rapid growth when plants are most susceptible to infection. (c) do not apply calcium-chelating foliar fertilizers (EDTA, DTPA chelates) in combination with sucker-control agents during very hot weather, as these can transiently suppress the N gene HR response and allow TMV to become systemic even in N-gene-resistant cultivars. (d) for non-resistant cigar-wrapper tobacco, implement a 4-5 year crop rotation completely out of all solanaceous crops (tobacco, tomato, pepper, potato, eggplant) to eliminate any small TMV carryover in soil debris. (5) THERE ARE NO CURATIVE TREATMENTS: as noted earlier, no chemical (antiviral) or biological treatment has ever been demonstrated to eliminate TMV from a systemically infected plant or to prevent symptom development after TMV infection has occurred. Products marketed as 'plant defense elicitors' (acibenzolar-S-methyl, ASM; chitosan oligomers; Reynoutria sachalinensis extract; β-aminobutyric acid; BABA) or 'antiviral agents' (ribavirin, moroxydine hydrochloride, ningnanmycin, oligosaccharins) can sometimes reduce symptom severity by 10-30% if applied repeatedly BEFORE infection, but they are never a substitute for resistant cultivars, seed certification, and strict sanitation. (6) Infected-plant ROGUING: in fields of TMV-susceptible cigar-wrapper or oriental tobacco where < 5% of plants are infected, rogue (remove and incinerate / landfill) all symptomatic plants plus the 3 immediately adjacent plants on each side of every symptomatic plant, as soon as symptoms are detected; this practice can slow spread enough to preserve a commercial crop of high-value wrapper leaf. If incidence exceeds 10% of plants, roguing is no longer economically viable, and the remaining crop should be harvested early for whatever use can be made of it. (7) Post-harvest handling: cured tobacco leaf contaminated with TMV remains infectious for DECADES - meaning cured leaf from TMV-infected plants should be clearly labeled and never used as a 'source' of seed, nor allowed to come into contact with live tobacco or tomato transplants in future years.
